entries.title: CREATE TABLE — declare columns and types
entries.summary: Creates an empty table by naming each column and its type: `TEXT` for words, `REAL` for decimals, `INTEGER` for whole numbers.
entries.gotcha: Running `CREATE TABLE` twice fails with “table holdings already exists”. In a notebook, put `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS holdings;` first so the cell can be re-run.

entries.title: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS — start clean
entries.summary: Deletes a whole table (and its rows) if it is there, and does nothing if it is not, so a notebook cell can be run again and again.
entries.syntax: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS name;
entries.setup:
CREATE TABLE holdings (ticker TEXT, price REAL, chg REAL);
INSERT INTO holdings VALUES ('NVDA', 219.00, -3.42);
entries.setup_note: a holdings table with one row already in the database
entries.gotcha: It really deletes the data. `DROP TABLE` is for scratch tables you can rebuild, never for a table you cannot recreate.

entries.title: INSERT INTO — add rows
entries.summary: Adds one or more rows; values are listed in the same order as the table's columns.
entries.syntax:
INSERT INTO table VALUES (v1, v2, v3);
INSERT INTO table VALUES (v1, v2, v3), (v1, v2, v3);
entries.setup: CREATE TABLE holdings (ticker TEXT, price REAL, chg REAL);
entries.setup_note: an empty holdings table
entries.gotcha: Text goes in single quotes (`'NVDA'`), numbers do not. From Python, insert many rows at once with `executemany` and `?` placeholders instead of pasting values into the string.

entries.title: DELETE FROM — remove rows
entries.summary: Removes the rows that match a condition; without a `WHERE` it empties the whole table.
entries.syntax:
DELETE FROM table WHERE condition;
DELETE FROM table;              -- every row
entries.setup:
CREATE TABLE holdings (ticker TEXT, price REAL, chg REAL);
INSERT INTO holdings VALUES ('NVDA', 219.00, -3.42), ('AAPL', 146.00, -2.73), ('GOOG', 2829.27, -58.20);
entries.setup_note: a holdings table with three rows
entries.example:
DELETE FROM holdings WHERE ticker = 'AAPL';

SELECT * FROM holdings;
entries.gotcha: There is no undo. The notebooks use `DELETE FROM holdings;` right before re-inserting rows so a cell does not pile up duplicates each time it runs.

entries.title: SELECT * — every column, every row
entries.summary: The simplest query: `*` means all columns, and with no `WHERE` you get all rows.
entries.syntax: SELECT * FROM table;
entries.setup:
CREATE TABLE holdings (ticker TEXT, price REAL, chg REAL);
INSERT INTO holdings VALUES ('NVDA', 219.00, -3.42), ('AAPL', 146.00, -2.73), ('GOOG', 2829.27, -58.20);
entries.setup_note: a holdings table with three rows
entries.example: SELECT * FROM holdings;
entries.gotcha: On a big table `SELECT *` pulls everything into memory. Add `LIMIT 5` while exploring.

entries.title: SELECT a, b — pick columns
entries.summary: Name the columns you want, separated by commas, in the order you want them back.
entries.syntax: SELECT col1, col2 FROM table;
entries.setup:
CREATE TABLE holdings (ticker TEXT, price REAL, chg REAL);
INSERT INTO holdings VALUES ('NVDA', 219.00, -3.42), ('AAPL', 146.00, -2.73), ('GOOG', 2829.27, -58.20);
entries.setup_note: a holdings table with three rows
entries.example: SELECT ticker, price FROM holdings;
entries.gotcha: Column names are not quoted. `SELECT 'ticker' FROM holdings` returns the word ticker three times, not the column.

entries.title: WHERE — keep the rows that match
entries.summary: A condition after `WHERE` keeps only the rows for which it is true, exactly like a boolean mask in pandas.
entries.syntax:
SELECT ... FROM table WHERE condition;
-- comparisons: =  !=  <  <=  >  >=
entries.setup:
CREATE TABLE passengers (passenger_id INTEGER, survived INTEGER, pclass INTEGER, sex TEXT, age REAL, fare REAL, embarked TEXT);
INSERT INTO passengers VALUES
  (1, 0, 3, 'male',   22.0,  7.25, 'S'),
  (2, 1, 1, 'female', 38.0, 71.28, 'C'),
  (3, 1, 3, 'female', 26.0,  7.92, 'S'),
  (4, 1, 1, 'female', 35.0, 53.10, 'S'),
  (5, 0, 3, 'male',   35.0,  8.05, 'S'),
  (6, 0, 3, 'male',   NULL,  8.46, 'Q');
entries.setup_note: a passengers table with the first six Titanic rows
entries.gotcha: SQL compares with a single `=` (`WHERE pclass = 3`), and text goes in single quotes: `WHERE sex = 'female'`.

entries.title: WHERE … AND / OR — combine conditions
entries.summary: Join two conditions with `AND` (both must hold) or `OR` (either one).
entries.syntax:
WHERE condition1 AND condition2
WHERE condition1 OR condition2
entries.setup:
CREATE TABLE passengers (passenger_id INTEGER, survived INTEGER, pclass INTEGER, sex TEXT, age REAL, fare REAL, embarked TEXT);
INSERT INTO passengers VALUES
  (1, 0, 3, 'male',   22.0,  7.25, 'S'),
  (2, 1, 1, 'female', 38.0, 71.28, 'C'),
  (3, 1, 3, 'female', 26.0,  7.92, 'S'),
  (4, 1, 1, 'female', 35.0, 53.10, 'S'),
  (5, 0, 3, 'male',   35.0,  8.05, 'S'),
  (6, 0, 3, 'male',   NULL,  8.46, 'Q');
entries.setup_note: a passengers table with the first six Titanic rows
entries.example:
-- third-class passengers who survived
SELECT passenger_id, sex, age
FROM passengers
WHERE pclass = 3 AND survived = 1;
entries.gotcha: In SQL you write the words `AND` / `OR`; in pandas the same idea uses `&` / `|` with parentheses around each condition.

entries.title: ORDER BY — sort the result
entries.summary: Sorts the returned rows by a column, smallest first; add `DESC` for largest first.
entries.syntax:
SELECT ... FROM table ORDER BY col;        -- ascending
SELECT ... FROM table ORDER BY col DESC;   -- descending
entries.setup:
CREATE TABLE passengers (passenger_id INTEGER, survived INTEGER, pclass INTEGER, sex TEXT, age REAL, fare REAL, embarked TEXT);
INSERT INTO passengers VALUES
  (1, 0, 3, 'male',   22.0,  7.25, 'S'),
  (2, 1, 1, 'female', 38.0, 71.28, 'C'),
  (3, 1, 3, 'female', 26.0,  7.92, 'S'),
  (4, 1, 1, 'female', 35.0, 53.10, 'S'),
  (5, 0, 3, 'male',   35.0,  8.05, 'S'),
  (6, 0, 3, 'male',   NULL,  8.46, 'Q');
entries.setup_note: a passengers table with the first six Titanic rows
entries.gotcha: The clauses have a fixed order: `SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`. `ORDER BY` before `WHERE` is a syntax error.

entries.title: LIMIT — only the first n rows
entries.summary: Cuts the result down to the first n rows, SQL's version of `.head(n)`; with `ORDER BY` it gives you the top n.
entries.syntax:
SELECT ... FROM table LIMIT n;
SELECT ... FROM table ORDER BY col DESC LIMIT n;
entries.setup:
CREATE TABLE passengers (passenger_id INTEGER, survived INTEGER, pclass INTEGER, sex TEXT, age REAL, fare REAL, embarked TEXT);
INSERT INTO passengers VALUES
  (1, 0, 3, 'male',   22.0,  7.25, 'S'),
  (2, 1, 1, 'female', 38.0, 71.28, 'C'),
  (3, 1, 3, 'female', 26.0,  7.92, 'S'),
  (4, 1, 1, 'female', 35.0, 53.10, 'S'),
  (5, 0, 3, 'male',   35.0,  8.05, 'S'),
  (6, 0, 3, 'male',   NULL,  8.46, 'Q');
entries.setup_note: a passengers table with the first six Titanic rows
entries.example:
-- the three most expensive tickets
SELECT passenger_id, age, fare
FROM passengers
ORDER BY fare DESC
LIMIT 3;
entries.gotcha: `LIMIT` is always the last clause. Without `ORDER BY` you get the first n rows in whatever order the database stores them.

entries.title: AS — rename a column in the output
entries.summary: Gives a column, or a computed value, a readable name in the result; the table itself is not changed.
entries.syntax:
SELECT col AS new_name FROM table;
SELECT ROUND(AVG(col), 2) AS avg_col FROM table;
entries.setup:
CREATE TABLE holdings (ticker TEXT, price REAL, chg REAL);
INSERT INTO holdings VALUES ('NVDA', 219.00, -3.42), ('AAPL', 146.00, -2.73), ('GOOG', 2829.27, -58.20);
entries.setup_note: a holdings table with three rows
entries.example:
SELECT ticker AS symbol, price AS closing_price
FROM holdings;
entries.gotcha: Without `AS`, a computed column comes back with an ugly name such as `ROUND(AVG(fare), 2)`, which is awkward to use from pandas.

entries.title: IS NULL / IS NOT NULL — find missing values
entries.summary: A missing value in SQL is `NULL`, and you test for it with `IS NULL`; comparisons like `= NULL` never match.
entries.syntax:
WHERE col IS NULL
WHERE col IS NOT NULL
entries.setup:
CREATE TABLE passengers (passenger_id INTEGER, survived INTEGER, pclass INTEGER, sex TEXT, age REAL, fare REAL, embarked TEXT);
INSERT INTO passengers VALUES
  (1, 0, 3, 'male',   22.0,  7.25, 'S'),
  (2, 1, 1, 'female', 38.0, 71.28, 'C'),
  (3, 1, 3, 'female', 26.0,  7.92, 'S'),
  (4, 1, 1, 'female', 35.0, 53.10, 'S'),
  (5, 0, 3, 'male',   35.0,  8.05, 'S'),
  (6, 0, 3, 'male',   NULL,  8.46, 'Q');
entries.setup_note: a passengers table with the first six Titanic rows (one age is missing)
entries.gotcha: `WHERE age = NULL` returns nothing, ever. `NULL` is “unknown”, so it is not equal to anything, not even to another `NULL`. Aggregates such as `AVG` already skip `NULL`s.

entries.title: SELECT DISTINCT — unique values
entries.summary: Returns each different value once, like `.unique()` in pandas.
entries.syntax: SELECT DISTINCT col FROM table;
entries.setup:
CREATE TABLE passengers (passenger_id INTEGER, survived INTEGER, pclass INTEGER, sex TEXT, age REAL, fare REAL, embarked TEXT);
INSERT INTO passengers VALUES
  (1, 0, 3, 'male',   22.0,  7.25, 'S'),
  (2, 1, 1, 'female', 38.0, 71.28, 'C'),
  (3, 1, 3, 'female', 26.0,  7.92, 'S'),
  (4, 1, 1, 'female', 35.0, 53.10, 'S'),
  (5, 0, 3, 'male',   35.0,  8.05, 'S'),
  (6, 0, 3, 'male',   NULL,  8.46, 'Q');
entries.setup_note: a passengers table with the first six Titanic rows
entries.example: SELECT DISTINCT embarked FROM passengers;
entries.gotcha: `DISTINCT` applies to the whole row of selected columns: `SELECT DISTINCT pclass, sex` lists every different class-and-sex pair.

entries.title: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col)
entries.summary: `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(col)` counts the rows where that column is not `NULL`.
entries.syntax:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table;
SELECT COUNT(col) FROM table;
entries.setup:
CREATE TABLE passengers (passenger_id INTEGER, survived INTEGER, pclass INTEGER, sex TEXT, age REAL, fare REAL, embarked TEXT);
INSERT INTO passengers VALUES
  (1, 0, 3, 'male',   22.0,  7.25, 'S'),
  (2, 1, 1, 'female', 38.0, 71.28, 'C'),
  (3, 1, 3, 'female', 26.0,  7.92, 'S'),
  (4, 1, 1, 'female', 35.0, 53.10, 'S'),
  (5, 0, 3, 'male',   35.0,  8.05, 'S'),
  (6, 0, 3, 'male',   NULL,  8.46, 'Q');
entries.setup_note: a passengers table with the first six Titanic rows (one age is missing)
entries.example: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n_rows, COUNT(age) AS n_ages FROM passengers;
entries.gotcha: pandas' `.count()` behaves like `COUNT(col)`, so a SQL `COUNT(*)` and a pandas count can legitimately disagree by exactly the number of missing values.

entries.title: AVG, MIN, MAX, SUM and ROUND
entries.summary: Summary functions collapse a column into one number; `ROUND(x, 2)` tidies the decimals.
entries.syntax:
SELECT AVG(col), MIN(col), MAX(col), SUM(col) FROM table;
SELECT ROUND(AVG(col), 2) AS avg_col FROM table;
entries.setup:
CREATE TABLE passengers (passenger_id INTEGER, survived INTEGER, pclass INTEGER, sex TEXT, age REAL, fare REAL, embarked TEXT);
INSERT INTO passengers VALUES
  (1, 0, 3, 'male',   22.0,  7.25, 'S'),
  (2, 1, 1, 'female', 38.0, 71.28, 'C'),
  (3, 1, 3, 'female', 26.0,  7.92, 'S'),
  (4, 1, 1, 'female', 35.0, 53.10, 'S'),
  (5, 0, 3, 'male',   35.0,  8.05, 'S'),
  (6, 0, 3, 'male',   NULL,  8.46, 'Q');
entries.setup_note: a passengers table with the first six Titanic rows
entries.example:
SELECT ROUND(AVG(fare), 2) AS avg_fare,
       MIN(fare)           AS min_fare,
       MAX(fare)           AS max_fare,
       ROUND(SUM(fare), 2) AS total_fare
FROM passengers;
entries.gotcha: The mean of a 0/1 column is a proportion: `AVG(survived)` is the survival rate, no extra work needed.

entries.title: GROUP BY — one summary line per group
entries.summary: Collapses the rows into one line per distinct value of a column and computes the summaries inside each group, SQL's `groupby().agg()`.
entries.setup:
CREATE TABLE passengers (passenger_id INTEGER, survived INTEGER, pclass INTEGER, sex TEXT, age REAL, fare REAL, embarked TEXT);
INSERT INTO passengers VALUES
  (1, 0, 3, 'male',   22.0,  7.25, 'S'),
  (2, 1, 1, 'female', 38.0, 71.28, 'C'),
  (3, 1, 3, 'female', 26.0,  7.92, 'S'),
  (4, 1, 1, 'female', 35.0, 53.10, 'S'),
  (5, 0, 3, 'male',   35.0,  8.05, 'S'),
  (6, 0, 3, 'male',   NULL,  8.46, 'Q');
entries.setup_note: a passengers table with the first six Titanic rows
entries.example:
SELECT pclass,
       COUNT(*)                AS n_passengers,
       ROUND(AVG(survived), 3) AS survival_rate,
       ROUND(AVG(fare), 2)     AS avg_fare
FROM passengers
GROUP BY pclass
ORDER BY pclass;
entries.gotcha: Every selected column must be either the grouping column or wrapped in a summary function. `SELECT pclass, fare … GROUP BY pclass` is ambiguous: which fare?

entries.title: HAVING — filter the groups
entries.summary: `WHERE` filters rows before grouping; `HAVING` filters the groups after the summaries are computed.
entries.syntax:
SELECT group_col, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM table
GROUP BY group_col
HAVING COUNT(*) > k;
entries.setup:
CREATE TABLE passengers (passenger_id INTEGER, survived INTEGER, pclass INTEGER, sex TEXT, age REAL, fare REAL, embarked TEXT);
INSERT INTO passengers VALUES
  (1, 0, 3, 'male',   22.0,  7.25, 'S'),
  (2, 1, 1, 'female', 38.0, 71.28, 'C'),
  (3, 1, 3, 'female', 26.0,  7.92, 'S'),
  (4, 1, 1, 'female', 35.0, 53.10, 'S'),
  (5, 0, 3, 'male',   35.0,  8.05, 'S'),
  (6, 0, 3, 'male',   NULL,  8.46, 'Q');
entries.setup_note: a passengers table with the first six Titanic rows
entries.example:
-- ports with more than one passenger
SELECT embarked, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM passengers
GROUP BY embarked
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
entries.gotcha: `WHERE COUNT(*) > 1` is an error: `WHERE` runs before the counting exists. Conditions on a summary belong in `HAVING`.

entries.title: LEFT JOIN … ON — the SQL cousin of merge
entries.summary: Glues a second table onto the first by matching a shared key column; `LEFT JOIN` keeps every row of the left table, like `pd.merge(how="left")`.
entries.syntax:
SELECT a.col, b.col
FROM left_table AS a
LEFT JOIN right_table AS b
  ON a.key = b.key;
entries.setup_note: seven Titanic passengers (one with no port recorded) plus a 3-row ports lookup table
entries.example:
SELECT p.passenger_id, p.embarked, o.port_name, o.country
FROM passengers AS p
LEFT JOIN ports AS o
  ON p.embarked = o.embarked;
entries.output:
passenger_id  embarked   port_name   country
------------  --------  -----------  -------
           1  S         Southampton  England
           2  C         Cherbourg    France
           3  S         Southampton  England
           4  S         Southampton  England
           5  S         Southampton  England
           6  Q         Queenstown   Ireland
          62  NULL      NULL         NULL
entries.gotcha: Passenger 62 has no port, so the join fills her port columns with `NULL` instead of dropping her. Always check the row count after a join.

entries.title: INNER JOIN — only the rows that match
entries.summary: Keeps only rows whose key appears in both tables; unmatched rows silently vanish.
entries.setup_note: seven Titanic passengers (one with no port recorded) plus a 3-row ports lookup table
entries.output:
passenger_id  embarked   port_name
------------  --------  -----------
           1  S         Southampton
           2  C         Cherbourg
           3  S         Southampton
           4  S         Southampton
           5  S         Southampton
           6  Q         Queenstown
n_inner
-------
      6
n_left
------
     7
entries.gotcha: Plain `JOIN` means `INNER JOIN`. If a count shrinks after a join, rows with an unmatched or missing key were dropped, which is what `how="inner"` does in pandas too.

entries.title: Table aliases: passengers AS p
entries.summary: A short nickname for a table lets you write `p.fare` instead of `passengers.fare`, which matters once two tables share column names.
entries.syntax:
FROM passengers AS p
LEFT JOIN ports AS o ON p.embarked = o.embarked
entries.setup_note: three Titanic passengers plus the ports lookup table
entries.example:
-- both tables have a column called embarked: the alias says which one you mean
SELECT p.passenger_id, p.embarked, o.embarked AS port_code, o.port_name
FROM passengers AS p
LEFT JOIN ports AS o ON p.embarked = o.embarked;
entries.output:
passenger_id  embarked  port_code   port_name
------------  --------  ---------  -----------
           1  S         S          Southampton
           2  C         C          Cherbourg
           3  S         S          Southampton
entries.gotcha: Once you alias a table you must use the alias: after `FROM passengers AS p`, writing `passengers.fare` is an error.

entries.title: Join and aggregate in one query
entries.summary: A join can feed straight into `GROUP BY`, so a lookup table's labels become the group names of a summary.
entries.syntax:
SELECT b.label, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(a.value) AS avg_value
FROM a
LEFT JOIN b ON a.key = b.key
GROUP BY b.label
ORDER BY n DESC;
entries.setup_note: six Titanic passengers plus the ports lookup table
entries.example:
SELECT o.port_name,
       COUNT(*)                  AS n_passengers,
       ROUND(AVG(p.fare), 2)     AS avg_fare,
       ROUND(AVG(p.survived), 3) AS survival_rate
FROM passengers AS p
LEFT JOIN ports AS o ON p.embarked = o.embarked
GROUP BY o.port_name
ORDER BY n_passengers DESC;
entries.output:
port_name   n_passengers  avg_fare  survival_rate
-----------  ------------  --------  -------------
Southampton             4     19.08            0.5
Queenstown              1      8.46            0.0
Cherbourg               1     71.28            1.0
entries.gotcha: You can `ORDER BY` an alias you defined in `SELECT` (`n_passengers`), but you cannot use it in `WHERE`.

entries.title: List the tables: sqlite_master
entries.summary: SQLite keeps its own catalog in a table called `sqlite_master`; query it to see which tables exist and how they were created.
entries.syntax:
SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table';
SELECT sql  FROM sqlite_master WHERE name = 'table_name';
entries.setup:
CREATE TABLE passengers (passenger_id INTEGER, survived INTEGER, pclass INTEGER, sex TEXT, age REAL, fare REAL, embarked TEXT);
CREATE TABLE ports (embarked TEXT, port_name TEXT, country TEXT);
entries.setup_note: two empty tables
entries.example:
SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table';

SELECT sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE name = 'ports';
entries.output:
name
----------
passengers
ports
                              sql
----------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE ports (embarked TEXT, port_name TEXT, country TEXT)
entries.gotcha: The catalog is read-only. To change a table, use `CREATE`, `DROP` or `ALTER TABLE`, not an `UPDATE` on `sqlite_master`.

entries.title: The sqlite3 command-line shell
entries.summary: `sqlite3 file.db` opens (or creates) a database file in the terminal, where you type SQL ending in `;` and dot-commands such as `.tables` and `.q`.
entries.syntax:
$ sqlite3 stocks.db          # open or create the file; the prompt becomes sqlite>
sqlite> .databases            # which file is open
sqlite> .tables               # list tables
sqlite> SELECT * FROM holdings;
sqlite> .q                    # quit
entries.output:
holdings
NVDA|219.0|-3.42
AAPL|146.0|-2.73
-rw-r--r--  1 student  staff  8192 Sep  4 15:42 stocks.db
entries.gotcha: Inside the shell every SQL statement must end with a semicolon or it waits for more input. Dot-commands (`.tables`, `.q`) take no semicolon.
entries.output_note: The last line is `ls -l` on the new database file; its size, date and time will differ on your machine.

entries.title: pandas ↔ SQL, side by side
entries.summary: The same handful of ideas in both languages. Learn one, translate the other.
entries.syntax:
task                pandas                                      SQL
----------------    ------------------------------------------  -----------------------------------
all rows & columns  df                                          SELECT * FROM t
pick columns        df[["a", "b"]]                              SELECT a, b FROM t
filter rows         df[df["x"] > 5]                             SELECT * FROM t WHERE x > 5
two conditions      df[(df.x > 5) & (df.y == 1)]                ... WHERE x > 5 AND y = 1
sort                df.sort_values("x", ascending=False)        ... ORDER BY x DESC
first rows          df.head(5)                                  ... LIMIT 5
count rows          df.shape[0]                                 SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t
group summary       df.groupby("g")["x"].mean()                 SELECT g, AVG(x) FROM t GROUP BY g
join tables         pd.merge(a, b, on="k", how="left")          FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
rename output       df.rename(columns={"x": "y"})               SELECT x AS y FROM t
entries.gotcha: One real difference: `COUNT(*)` counts rows, pandas' `.count()` counts non-missing values. Write the same question both ways and check that the answers agree.
